title: Entering another body; levitation; radiance (3.38–3.45)
hook: the boldest powers in the book, read the way the classical commentators read them, inside a world where mind and body are both part of nature
carry: read as the tradition reads it

segments.voice: Yesterday: upasarga, and your line, the warning. Gold on the podium, a weight in the water. Did you take one medal off today? Day four hundred seventy-four.
screen: `THE WARNING — A MEDAL IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells a story about the great teacher Shankara. He has just won a famous debate against the scholar Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife, the brilliant Ubhaya Bharati, takes up the challenge herself. She asks him about love between husband and wife. Shankara, a lifelong monk, has no answer. So he asks for time. He leaves his own body in a cave, guarded by his students, and enters the body of a king who has just died. He lives as that king for a while, learns what he needs, and comes back. Today's sutras name exactly that power, and others just as startling.
screen: `A DEBATE ABOUT LOVE.` → `A MONK WITH NO ANSWER.` → `HE ENTERS A KING'S BODY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.38: by loosening what binds the mind to one body, and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another body. Para-sharira-avesha. Sutra 3.39: by mastering udana, the upward-moving breath, there's no contact with water, mud or thorns, and the body rises. Levitation. The commentary adds that this mastery also lets one choose the moment of leaving the body at death. Sutra 3.40: by mastering samana, the breath at the body's center, radiance, a glow. Sutra 3.41: samyama on the ear and space, divine hearing. Sutra 3.42: on the body and space, and on the lightness of cotton, moving through the air. How do you hear this? A few days ago, with the elephant, the line was read as metaphor. Today's line asks for something different: read it the way the tradition reads it. And the classical commentators read it as real. That isn't as strange inside their world as it sounds in ours. In the Samkhya-Yoga picture, the mind isn't a ghost in a machine. Mind and body are both made of nature, prakriti, the mind just far subtler. So a mind that has mastered its own subtle stuff might master the coarser stuff too. Only the seer stands outside nature, and the seer has no interest in levitating. Which brings back yesterday. Sutra 3.37 called the powers just before it obstacles in samadhi, and many teachers hear that warning over this whole list. Shankara, in the story, didn't stay a king. He learned what he came for, and went back to his own body, and his work.
screen: `PARA-SHARIRA-AVESHA: ANOTHER BODY.` · `UDANA MASTERED: THE BODY RISES.` · `SAMANA MASTERED: RADIANCE.` · `MIND AND BODY, BOTH OF NATURE.` · then, large: `READ AS THE TRADITION READS IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice feels lightness, nothing more. Sit steady and easy. With each in-breath, notice the slight lift in the chest and the crown, as if the body rose a little. With each out-breath, notice it settle. Then picture a tuft of cotton, light enough to drift. Let the body feel just a little lighter, without straining for anything. If the mind reaches for something dramatic, smile at it, and come back to the plain breath. The bell holds the time.
Para-sharira-avesha, entering another's body. The first of today's powers, with levitation and radiance, which the classical commentators read as real attainments of mastery.

Your line: read as the tradition reads it. Today, when something in an old story sounds impossible, ask first how it makes sense inside that story's world, before deciding what you think. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: The classical commentaries on the Yoga Sutras treat these powers as real results of mastery within the Samkhya-Yoga view of nature, and Hindu stories of saints, such as the traditional life of Shankara, tell of such powers being used briefly and set aside.

myth: the classical commentators read these powers as metaphor only
they read them as real attainments of mastery.
in Samkhya-Yoga, the mind is part of nature like the body
both are prakriti; the mind is subtler. only the seer stands outside.
in the story, Shankara stays a king
he learns what he came for and returns to his own body.

fork.setup: you're Shankara. a debate turns to a subject you've never lived. what do you do?
options: ask for time, enter a king's body, learn, and come back.
fork.reveal: in the traditional story, he leaves his body in a cave, lives as a king who had just died, and returns to answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: these are fairy tales in a philosophy book.
what it means: in the commentators' world, mind and body are both nature, so mastery of the subtle can reach the coarse.
what a scholar hears: 3.38 para-sharira-avesha; udana-jaya and utkranti (3.39); samana-jaya and jvalana (3.40); numbering varies by one across editions.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): 3.37 refers to the powers of 3.36, so 'every one of these, says 3.37' overstated it; the teach now says many teachers extend the warning. The hook now places Ubhaya Bharati correctly (Mandana Mishra's wife, who challenged Shankara after his win). The carry no longer assumes the listener is outside the tradition ('another culture's story').

The Shankara story (debate with Ubhaya Bharati, entering King Amaruka's body) is from the traditional hagiographies (e.g. the Madhaviya Shankara Digvijaya), framed as 'tradition tells'. Confirm details.
Bhashya on 3.39: utkranti read as rising and as departure at will at death; confirm.
The outline's range runs to 3.45; 3.43–3.45 are left for tomorrow's day on the elements to avoid overlap.
Samkhya-Yoga account of mind as subtle prakriti: confirm the framing.
